modules.briefing: Trailhead Outdoors is a small fictional shop. Its product search takes your words and builds a database query out of them — directly, with no parameterization. Start with a normal search, watch the shape of the results, and then think about what happens when your input stops being a search term and starts being query syntax. Everything here is fictional: a fake in-memory catalog and a fake users table with invented accounts.
modules.fix: Parameterize every query — placeholders, never string concatenation. Give the database account least privilege: read-only on the catalog, with no access to the accounts table from the search path. Validate input shape on the way in, and never echo raw query structure in error messages.
hints: Start with a normal search — a product name you know, like Trail. Watch what comes back and how the results are shaped.
The search builds its query from your words. Try a value that changes the shape of the query instead of the search term — a quote character is the classic probe.
A tautology in the right place makes the filter true for every row. If the catalog suddenly returns everything, you have proven the input reaches the query.
The query has more than one table behind it. A UNION lets one query return rows from another table — think about which table holds the accounts.
Combine the pieces: break out of the search term, UNION in a second SELECT over the accounts table, and comment out the tail. The users table is the target.
modules.objective: Use the product search to dump the fake users table — usernames and emails — without logging in.
modules.root_cause: The search built its database query by concatenating the user's words into the query string. There was no parameterization and no allowlist, so user input became query syntax — the classic injection root cause. The search path could also reach the accounts table, so one flaw exposed two tables.
modules.source: Classic web vulnerability training — original mock scenario
modules.title: The Loose Query

modules.briefing: Trailhead Outdoors lets shoppers leave product reviews, and the product page shows those reviews exactly as they were written — no encoding, no sanitization. Whatever is stored gets rendered as live markup in every visitor's browser. Your proof must be harmless: a marker that only sets a practice flag in the page, with no network calls and no exfiltration. The page itself must run it.
modules.fix: Encode output on render — build DOM nodes with text content, never raw markup insertion for user content. Sanitize rich content with an allowlist if formatting is required, and add a strict Content Security Policy as a backstop. Treat stored user content as untrusted on every render, not just on input.
hints: Read the existing reviews and look at how the page shows them — is the text encoded, or dropped into the page raw?
Post a review with harmless markup — bold text or an image tag — and see whether it lands unencoded.
If markup lands raw, an event handler on a broken image is the classic stored-XSS probe: it runs when the page renders, with no click needed.
Your payload only needs to set the practice flag — nothing else. No network, no exfiltration: the flag is the whole proof.
Post the review carrying the flag-setter, reload the product view, and watch the app detect the flag and mark the objective complete.
modules.objective: Get a harmless marker to execute when the product page renders your stored review — the page itself must run it, with no network calls.
modules.root_cause: Reviews were stored and rendered without any output encoding — the page inserted review text into the document as live markup, so stored text became stored code in every visitor's browser. Input validation alone would not have fixed it: the flaw was on render.
modules.source: Classic web vulnerability training — original mock scenario
modules.title: The Raw Review

modules.briefing: Trailhead Outdoors lets you fetch a product image by URL — handy for sellers. The URL you supply is passed straight through with no validation and no allowlist. Behind the shop sit mock internal routes that no shopper should ever reach. The containment rule of this trainer: the fetcher only ever resolves to handlers inside this same app — it never makes a real outbound request. The flaw is real in logic, and physically contained.
modules.fix: Allowlist fetch targets to the image host and path prefix, resolve and re-validate after redirects, block private, loopback, and link-local ranges, and run fetchers in an isolated network segment with no route to internal services. In this trainer the fetch is contained in-process — in a real app the same rules apply at the network layer.
hints: Try the feature normally first — point it at a product image path and see what comes back.
The feature takes a URL and fetches whatever it is given. Ask yourself: what addresses live behind the app that a shopper should never reach?
Internal routes answer on paths, not on public URLs. The fetcher resolves what you give it — try the internal status path directly.
A full URL with the internal path in it resolves the same way. The flaw is the missing check, not the address format.
Fetch the internal status route through the image feature and read the fake instance metadata it returns.
modules.objective: Use the image-fetch feature to reach the mock internal status route — without the app ever making a real outbound request.
modules.root_cause: The image feature accepted a caller-supplied URL and resolved it with no allowlist and no check against internal addresses. User input chose the fetch target — the definition of SSRF. The internal routes trusted any caller that could reach them.
modules.source: Classic web vulnerability training — original mock scenario
modules.title: The Helpful Fetcher

modules.briefing: Trailhead Outdoors changes the account email behind a plain GET link — no form, no anti-forgery check, and the session is ambient, so any page the account holder visits can issue the request with their authority. Try the change yourself first with a single GET request. Then run the victim simulation: a mock malicious page loads while carlos is the visitor, and its hidden request fires without him doing anything.
modules.fix: State changes require POST with an unguessable per-session anti-forgery value, validated server-side. Add SameSite cookies and Origin/Referer checks as defense in depth, and never put a state change behind a GET request.
hints: Look at the account page: what does the email change look like — a form, or a plain link?
A state change behind a GET link can be triggered by anything that makes the browser issue the request — including an image tag on another page.
Try the change yourself with a plain GET request carrying the new address. No form needed, no check in the way.
Now prove the victim flow: the simulation loads a mock malicious page as carlos, and the page's hidden request fires with his session.
Run the victim simulation and watch the email change without carlos doing anything at all.
modules.objective: Change the account email with a single GET request — no form, no anti-forgery check — then prove the victim flow: a visit to a mock malicious page does it too.
modules.owasp: A01:2021 Broken Access Control · Cross-Site Request Forgery
modules.root_cause: A state-changing action lived behind a GET request with no anti-forgery check and an ambient session. Any page the victim visited could issue the request with the victim's authority — the browser, not the user, performed the action.
modules.source: Classic web vulnerability training — original mock scenario
modules.title: The One-Click Email Change
